entries.title: Swallowed PostgREST errors silently reverse decisions in the money and permission paths

source.ref: ADR-1198, the sweep that followed LIVE-152

entries.detail:
LIVE-152 was one instance of a pattern: `const { data } = await db()...` with `error` neither destructured nor checked. A PostgREST error arrives in `error`, not as a throw, so a try/catch documented as "FAIL-SAFE on any error" does not engage - the code silently takes the data-is-null branch instead.

83 such reads exist. Most degrade to an empty list, which is harmless. These do not, ranked by how wrong the answer is:
  1. lib/commerce/reviews.ts:173 - a failed read defaults status to 'visible', UN-HIDING a review an operator moderated. The comment three lines above says moderation must be durable "else moderation is trivially reversible by the author".
  2. lib/billing/space-subscriptions.ts:155 - priorSubscriptionId null means a canceled subscription never lapses founding status, so a Space keeps a founding rate it stopped paying for.
  3. lib/billing/tickets.ts:382 and lib/commerce/checkout.ts:75 - membership_tier null prices at the free rung, charging a Crew seller 10% instead of 8%.
  4. lib/billing/checkout.ts:56,220 and space-plan-checkout.ts:246 and bundle-checkout.ts:65 - stripe_customer_id null mints a DUPLICATE Stripe customer per checkout; at :220 createBillingPortal tells a paying member they have no billing to manage.
  5. lib/billing/tickets.ts:211 - tier defaults to 'free' behind the member_only gate, denying a paying Crew member their own ticket.
  6. lib/pricing/gamification-access.ts:76 - a full-access paid member is downgraded to earn_only.
  7. lib/pricing/dunning.ts:36 - fails OPEN: a past_due member never sees the recovery banner and keeps access.

Not a mechanical sweep: each needs a direction decided (fail open or closed) and stated. Do the money ones first.

verify.note: Passes when the four highest-severity files destructure `error` at all. A coarse gate on purpose: it measures that someone looked, and each fix still has to choose a direction.

entries.title: A synced Stripe price id carries no account or livemode, so a foreign price is indistinguishable from a missing one
entries.detail:
pricing_stripe_prices.stripe_price_id is a bare text column. Nothing records WHICH Stripe account or livemode minted it, and resolveStripePriceId does no validation - the id goes straight into checkout.sessions.create. If the platform's secret key is ever rotated to a different account (a new license, a test/live swap), every row silently points at a foreign price and Stripe answers "No such price", which is indistinguishable from a transient outage: viaStripe renders "Stripe could not complete that just now" on both.

billingEnabled() is only "is STRIPE_SECRET_KEY set" - it does not care which account. Verified 2026-09-04: all four plan rows (business_base and collective_base, month and year) are present and unarchived, synced 2026-08-19, so nothing is broken TODAY. The gap is that nothing would tell us if it were.

ADR-1085's own lesson applies - the guard belongs before the write rather than in a report afterwards: record the account id and livemode on the row at sync time and refuse to resolve a row minted by a different account than the live key.

verify.cmd: node -e "const fs=require('fs');const s=fs.readFileSync('lib/billing/pricing-prices.ts','utf8');process.exit(/livemode|stripe_account/.test(s)?0:1)"
verify.note: Passes when a synced price row records the account or livemode it came from, so a foreign id can be named rather than guessed at.

entries.title: Spec every capability bundle, and re-review the 22-key function registry beside it
entries.detail:
Owner ruling: before any bundle ships, write a full spec per bundle and review the FUNCTION REGISTRY at the same time. The two are one decision. A bundle is defined by what it omits, so naming the omissions is a statement about lib/spaces/functions.ts — whether 22 keys are the right 22, whether any should merge, split or retire, and which are genuinely optional rather than structural.

WHY THIS BLOCKS LIVE-149 RATHER THAN THE OTHER WAY AROUND. The mechanism is finished and proven: CAPABILITY_BUNDLES + nextBlobsForBundle + setSpaceBundle, with the three-state entitlement read underneath so a bundle can subtract a tool from a Space whose plan pays for it. What does not exist is curation, and wiring provision to a registry holding one pass-through row would put a permanent no-op branch in the Space-creation path, the highest-risk path in the product.

THE EVIDENCE TO BRING. Of 21 real operator Spaces roughly 18 are solo wellness practitioners, and coaches-and-healers is the only /for/ door that has produced a customer. That is the one bundle with anything behind it; every other would be a guess, which is exactly why the mechanism shipped without curation.

DELIVERABLE: a row per bundle in lib/pricing/bundles.ts with its function list and any role floors, plus a recorded decision for each of the 22 function keys (keep / merge / retire / make structural). LIVE-149's provision call ships in the same change as the first curated bundle, never before it.

verify.evidence: CAPABILITY_BUNDLES holds more than the pass-through row, each bundle has a written spec, and every function key carries a recorded keep/merge/retire decision.

entries.title: The RLS-bypass justifications are byte-present but no longer attached to the entries they justify
entries.detail:
A whole-file lexicographic sort has run over scripts/admin-client-baseline.txt at some point, taking the 80-line comment block with it. Three independent proofs: 78 of the 79 adjacent comment pairs are in alphabetical order (the single exception is a hand-insert from 2026-09-04); the script's own five header lines, written in order 1-2-3-4-5, sit at lines 45/46/51/47/63, which is exactly their lexicographic order and no writer produces that; and the prose no longer parses — line 24 ends '...the autonomy ladder is' and its continuation sits at line 3.

So the reasoning for each RLS bypass is still in the file and no longer says which bypass it is about. Four commented lines that read like entries are also real live entries, i.e. surviving heads of shredded paragraphs.

SCAN-537 stopped it getting worse (--update preserves the block now). This row is the repair, and it is NOT mechanical: reassembling 80 shredded lines into per-entry paragraphs needs someone who knows the tenancy model to decide which sentence belongs to which bypass. git log on the file is 3 commits deep and the 823 lines arrived in one commit, so the pre-sort original cannot be recovered from this repository.

Worth considering alongside: make --update REFUSE when the header's line count would shrink, as belt and braces. That changes CLI behaviour, so it is a decision rather than a patch.

verify.evidence: Each justification paragraph in scripts/admin-client-baseline.txt sits with the entry it explains, and the prose parses end to end.

entries.title: The packed-cache estimate ran low on all three paired readings of 2026-09-05, and the upload reached 1.41 GB
entries.detail: Scan two, phase D6 (2026-09-05), measured on the merge run itself. check:cache-budget predicts packed size as raw x PACKED_PER_RAW = 0.53, and ADR-1113 settled that constant on paired readings accurate to 1% and rounded toward firing the trim EARLY. Three paired readings the same day all ran the other way: 1.31 predicted / 1.31 uploaded (main at 08e6169), 1.36 / 1.38 (main at 67ada96), and 1.35 / 1.41 (main at e2d6107). The last is 94% of the 1.50 GB ceiling and at the trim point, and a 4% low estimate is the direction that costs a BUILD rather than a CPU minute, because the trim fires after the cache is already over. The mix has moved: .next/cache grew 1428 to 1522 MiB across the day while node_modules held at 921 MiB, so the cache is more compiler-heavy than the mix 0.53 was derived on. Re-derive the constant from these readings (the implied ratio is near 0.55) and raise it, which fires the trim earlier; do NOT lower it. The change belongs in its own PR with the green build that proves it, per the rule that a threshold ships beside its measurement.

verify.evidence: 2026-09-05: three paired readings from production build logs (dpl_Cas653f4, dpl_6gcnzawu, dpl_AUFhqsQt): predicted 1.31/1.36/1.35 GB against uploaded 1.31/1.38/1.41 GB. Closes when a re-derived PACKED_PER_RAW ships with a paired reading that agrees within 1% on the current mix.
